entry: Machine for copying documents and other images onto [[Paper|paper]] or plastic film. Most modern photocopiers use xerography, a dry process in which electrostatic charges on a light-sensitive photoreceptor attract toner particles, which are transferred to the paper and fused with heat or pressure. Xerography gradually replaced verifax, photostat, carbon paper and mimeograph copying in offices. In the 1980s, high-end machines began combining copying with [[Fax|fax]], scanning and network printing, and photocopying remains widely used in business, education and [[Government|government]]. Low-end color machines came to dominate the home-office market as prices fell during the 1990s. Patent attorney Chester Carlson invented the process in 1938. Between 1939 and 1944 he was turned down by over 20 companies, including [[IBM]] and [[General Electric]]. The Battelle Memorial Institute in [[Columbus, Ohio]] then helped refine it. Haloid, later Xerox Corporation, introduced the first xerographic copier, the Model A, in 1949.

Emission of [[Electron|electrons]] from a material when [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] such as light strikes it. The ejected electrons are called photoelectrons. Classical electromagnetism predicted that dim light would eventually transfer enough energy to release electrons, but experiments showed that emission occurs only above a material-specific threshold frequency, regardless of intensity or exposure time. Increasing intensity raises the number of electrons emitted but not their energy. In 1905, [[Albert Einstein]] proposed that light consists of discrete energy packets, later named [[Photon|photons]] by [[Gilbert N. Lewis]]. [[Robert Millikan]] verified the relationship experimentally in 1916, and Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. The effect underpins solar cells, photodetectors and photomultiplier tubes.

Strip or sheet of transparent base coated with a [[Gelatin|gelatin]] emulsion of light-sensitive silver halide crystals, used to take photographs. Exposure to light creates an invisible latent image, which chemical development converts into a visible picture. Unmodified crystals respond only to blue light until sensitizing [[Dye|dyes]] were adsorbed onto them, producing orthochromatic and then panchromatic films, which are sensitive to all [[Visible spectrum|visible]] colors. Special films can also be sensitive to [[Infrared|infrared]] light. Black-and-white film has one layer of crystals, which develop into metallic silver. Color film has at least three sensitive layers, and by-products of development form colored dyes with color couplers. Later films, such as Kodacolor II, had as many as 12 emulsion layers. The rise of digital imaging shifted film to a niche role in artistic and archival work.

[[Journalism]] that uses images to tell a news story, usually still images but sometimes broadcast video. Unlike related forms such as documentary and war photography, it is bound by a rigid ethical framework that demands an honest, impartial approach in strictly journalistic terms. Photojournalists often decide instantly while facing physical danger, bad weather and large crowds. Roger Fenton's photographs of the [[Crimean War]] were printed in the *Illustrated London News*, and photographs of the [[American Civil War]] were engraved before publication. John Thomson's monthly *Street Life in London* (1876–77) made printed photographs the main medium for conveying information. The first halftone reproduction of a news photograph appeared in the *Daily Graphic* in New York in 1880. *Life* magazine, launched in 1936, used photo-essays to expose the hardships of the [[Great Depression]] and the atrocities of [[World War II]].

Instrument for measuring quantities such as luminous flux, illuminance or luminance. Early photometry relied on visual estimation, comparing the luminous flux of a source with a standard source. By 1861, three types were in common use: Rumford's photometer, which compared the depths of shadows cast by two lights; Ritchie's photometer, which compared equal illumination of surfaces; and devices based on the extinction of shadows, considered the most precise. Most modern photometers convert [[Light|light]] into an electric current with photoresistors, photodiodes or photomultipliers. Some count individual [[Photon|photons]], which suits very low light levels. Photometers determine exposure in [[Photography|photography]] and, in [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopy]], the concentration of substances in a solution.

Astronomical technique for measuring the [[Flux|flux]] or intensity of light from [[Astronomical object|celestial objects]]. Electronic [[Photometer|photometers]] used with a [[Telescope|telescope]] are calibrated against standard stars of known intensity and color to measure the [[Apparent magnitude|apparent magnitude]] of objects. Observations use standard filters that define a photometric system, such as the UBV system. Differential photometry compares a target with nearby stars, and a plot of magnitude against time produces a light curve, which reveals the physical processes behind changes in the brightness of [[Variable star|variable stars]]. Precision photoelectric photometers can measure starlight to around 0.001 magnitude. Surface photometry measures the brightness of extended objects such as [[Nebula|nebulae]] in magnitudes per square arcsecond. CCD cameras have largely replaced photoelectric photometers, which remain useful where fine time resolution is needed.

Group of one or more words functioning as a grammatical unit within a larger structure, such as a [[Sentence (linguistics)|sentence]]. A phrase can be a single word or a complete sentence. In "the squirrel is very happy," "the squirrel" is a [[Noun|noun]] phrase and "is very happy" a [[Verb|verb]] phrase, with "very happy" an adjective phrase. In most theories of [[Syntax|syntax]], a phrase is any group of words that plays a particular role in a sentence, whether or not it has special meaning. In common usage, a phrase is usually an idiom or fixed expression, such as "kick the bucket"; in [[Linguistics|linguistics]], these are called phrasemes. A phrase whose head is a noun is called a noun phrase. Theories of syntax differ in which word combinations count as phrases, and constituency and dependency trees can identify different numbers of phrases in the same sentence.

Ancient kingdom and civilization in west-central [[Anatolia]], centered on the Sangarios River in what is now [[Turkey]]. Legendary Phrygian kings included Gordias, whose Gordian Knot was later cut by [[Alexander the Great]], and Midas, who turned whatever he touched to gold. According to Homer's *Iliad*, Phrygians fought in the [[Trojan War]] as allies of the Trojans. Phrygian power peaked in the late 8th century BC under the historical king Midas, who dominated most of western and central Anatolia and rivaled Assyria and Urartu in the east. Cimmerians sacked the capital, Gordium, around 695 BC. Phrygia then came under [[Lydia]], Persia, Alexander and his Hellenistic successors, the [[Seleucid Empire]], Pergamon, the [[Roman Empire]] and the [[Byzantine Empire]]. Phrygians became Christian and Greek-speaking, and the name "Phrygia" passed out of use as a territorial designation after the Turkish conquest of Byzantine Anatolia.

Southern province of [[Thailand]] (pop., 2025: 432,464), consisting of Phuket Island, the country's largest island, and 32 smaller islands. Phuket lies off the west coast of mainland Thailand in the [[Andaman Sea]] and is linked to Phang Nga province by the Sarasin Bridge. At 547 sq km (211 sq mi), it is the second-smallest province in Thailand. The island lay on a historic trade route between India and China, and Portuguese, French, Dutch and English ships called there, though no European power colonized it. [[Tin|Tin]] and rubber once drove the economy, but [[Tourism|tourism]] is now its main source of income. The province has faced challenges including the [[Tsunami|2004 Indian Ocean tsunami]] and overdevelopment.

Study of the evolutionary relationships among organisms, inferred from heritable traits such as [[DNA]] sequences and morphology. Phylogenetic analyses produce a phylogenetic tree, a diagram of hypothesized relationships. A rooted tree indicates a hypothetical common ancestor, while an unrooted tree makes no assumption about the direction of character change. Methods include distance-based approaches, maximum parsimony, maximum likelihood and [[Bayesian inference]], which estimates posterior distributions of trees. Phylogenetic methods are used to study the clonal evolution of tumors in [[Cancer|cancer]] research, to screen related species for useful [[Venom|venom]] traits in drug discovery, and to assess DNA evidence in [[Forensic science|forensic science]]. [[HIV]] forensics can show whether two samples are related, but it cannot alone prove transmission or its direction.

[[Taxonomic rank]] below [[Kingdom (taxonomy)|kingdom]] and above class. Botany traditionally uses *division* instead, although the international code for algae, fungi and plants treats the terms as equivalent. Depending on definitions, the [[Animal|animal]] kingdom contains about 32 phyla, the [[Plant|plant]] kingdom about 14 and the [[Fungus|fungus]] kingdom about eight. [[Ernst Haeckel]] coined the term in 1866 from the Greek *phylon*, meaning race or stock. As molecular studies reveal relationships, phyla are merged or split. The bearded worms, first described as a phylum in the mid-20th century, were later found to be [[Annelid|annelids]].

Medical assessment for signs of [[Disease|disease]] in a patient. The examination usually follows a series of questions about the patient's medical history, and together they help determine a diagnosis and treatment plan. Routine examinations, often called annual physicals, are performed on asymptomatic patients for screening, usually by a primary care provider such as a pediatrician or family physician, and may include laboratory tests, ultrasound or mammography. A Cochrane Collaboration meta-study found that routine annual physicals did not measurably reduce the risk of illness or death and could lead to overdiagnosis and over-treatment. The American Cancer Society recommends a cancer-related check-up annually for men and women older than 40, and every three years for those older than 20. Some employers require a checkup before hiring.

State of health and [[Well-being|well-being]], including the ability to perform sports, occupational tasks and daily activities. It is generally achieved through proper [[Nutrition|nutrition]], moderate to vigorous [[Exercise|exercise]] and sufficient rest. Before the [[Industrial Revolution]], fitness meant the capacity to carry out the day's activities without undue fatigue. Health-related components include cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility and body composition. Skill-related components include balance, agility, coordination, power and speed. Fitness reduces the risk of cardiovascular conditions, type 2 diabetes and several cancers, and it can help treat [[Anxiety|anxiety]] and [[Depression (mood)|depression]]. The World Health Organization recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity weekly for adults, plus muscle-strengthening exercise on two or more days. Research suggests that many of exercise's benefits are mediated by myokines released by contracting muscles.

Branch of [[Geography|geography]] that studies processes and patterns in the natural environment, including the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and geosphere. It contrasts with [[Human geography|human geography]], which focuses on the built environment, and [[Technical geography|technical geography]], which concerns tools for analyzing spatial information. Its sub-branches include [[Geomorphology|geomorphology]], which studies landforms and the processes that shape them; [[Hydrology|hydrology]], which concerns water on and beneath the land surface; glaciology, the study of glaciers and ice sheets; [[Climatology|climatology]], which examines weather conditions averaged over long periods; and biogeography, which studies the geographic patterns of species distribution. Biogeography emerged through the work of [[Alfred Russel Wallace]]. The subfields are united by core processes, mainly tectonic or climatic.

Healthcare profession, also called physiotherapy, that promotes, maintains or restores physical function. Physical therapists treat illnesses or injuries that limit a person's ability to move, using exercise, manual therapy, traction, electrotherapy such as heat, cold and electricity, and assistive devices and prostheses. They also work to prevent loss of mobility through fitness and wellness programs. Specialties include musculoskeletal, orthopedic, cardiopulmonary, [[Neurology|neurology]], sports medicine, [[Geriatrics|geriatrics]] and [[Pediatrics|pediatrics]]. Physical therapists practice in clinics, hospitals, schools and workplaces, and in roles such as health policy and administration. The profession rose to prominence during World War I, when it rehabilitated wounded soldiers. In the United States, the Doctor of Physical Therapy degree became mandatory for entry by 2020.

Theories extending the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics to explain its deficiencies. The Standard Model cannot explain the strong CP problem, neutrino oscillations, matter–antimatter asymmetry, or the nature of [[Dark matter|dark matter]] and [[Dark energy|dark energy]]. It is also inconsistent with [[General relativity]], so one or both theories break down under conditions such as the Big Bang and black hole event horizons. Cosmological observations indicate that the Standard Model accounts for about 5% of the universe's mass-energy. Proposals include extensions through [[Supersymmetry]], such as the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, and novel explanations such as [[String theory]], M-theory and extra dimensions. Because many of these theories reproduce current phenomena, the choice among them can only be settled by experiment, such as searches at the [[Large Hadron Collider]].

[[Keyboard instrument]] in which felt-covered hammers strike strings when keys are pressed. Modern pianos have 88 keys tuned to equal temperament. The two main types are the grand piano, which offers better sound and key control, and the upright piano, which is smaller, cheaper and more commonly used. Most notes have three strings, and sustain pedals lift the dampers so that notes continue to sound. Invented around 1700 in Florence by [[Harpsichord|harpsichord]] maker Bartolomeo Cristofori, the early *fortepiano* allowed gradations of volume according to the force of touch. In the 19th century, a cast-iron frame allowed much greater string tension, giving grand pianos a more powerful sound and a longer sustain. The piano is widely used in classical, [[Jazz|jazz]] and popular music, and it is a familiar instrument in the Western world.

Set of 32 mature works for piano by [[Ludwig van Beethoven]], written between 1795 and 1822. Beethoven also wrote three sonatas at age 13, in 1782–83, which are usually excluded from the set. As a set, the sonatas comprise one of the most important collections in the history of music. They came to be seen as the first cycle of major piano pieces suited to both private and public performance. Hans von Bülow called them "The New Testament" of piano literature, with Johann Sebastian Bach's *The Well-Tempered Clavier* as the "Old Testament". The early sonatas were influenced by [[Joseph Haydn|Haydn]] and Mozart. The middle and late sonatas grew more daring in form and expression, and after the 20th sonata, published in 1805, Beethoven issued each new sonata as a single opus. The late sonatas incorporate fugal technique and depart radically from conventional sonata form.

[[Eating disorder]] involving compulsive craving or consumption of objects not normally intended as food. The term comes from the [[Latin]] word for the [[Eurasian magpie]], a bird known for opportunistic feeding. Under the DSM-5, standalone pica must persist for more than one month at a developmentally inappropriate age. It is most common in pregnant women, small children and people with developmental disorders such as [[Autism|autism]]. Complications include [[Lead|lead]] poisoning from paint, intestinal obstruction and infections from feces or soil. Pica is strongly associated with iron and zinc deficiency, and it often remits spontaneously in children and during pregnancy.

Racket sport in which two or four players hit a perforated plastic ball over a net with smooth-faced paddles. It was invented in 1965 as a children's backyard game on Bainbridge Island, [[Washington (state)|Washington]], and became the state's official sport in 2022. A player in the 7-foot non-volley zone, called the kitchen, may not strike the ball before it has bounced. Serves are underhand. The sport was the fastest-growing in the United States from 2021 through 2024. The Sports and Fitness Industry Association reported 24.3 million American players in 2025. More than 90% of professional players have a background in [[Tennis]].

Usually small [[Cucumber|cucumber]] preserved in [[Brine|brine]] or [[Vinegar|vinegar]] and left to ferment. It is commonly called a pickle in the [[United States]] and a gherkin in Britain. Brined pickles are fermented by lactobacilli that occur naturally on the cucumber's skin, in brine containing 20–40 grams of salt per liter. Pickled cucumbers were being made in the Tigris Valley around 2030 BC, and the U.S. government allocated 40% of the nation's pickle production to the armed forces during World War II. Pickled cucumbers are highly popular in the United States and are a delicacy in northern and eastern [[Europe]].

Process of preserving food by anaerobic fermentation in [[Brine|brine]] or immersion in [[Vinegar|vinegar]]. Pickling usually alters a food's texture and flavor. Pickling solutions are typically highly acidic, with a pH of 4.6 or lower, and high in salt, which prevents enzymes and most microorganisms from acting. Pickled food can last for months or years, and pickling does not require the complete sterility that [[Canning|canning]] does. Salt and temperature determine which bacteria dominate: at low salt and temperature *Leuconostoc mesenteroides* predominates, while at higher temperatures *Lactobacillus plantarum* produces mainly [[Lactic acid|lactic acid]]. Pickling with vinegar likely originated in ancient Persia and Mesopotamia around 2400 BCE. It was used to preserve food for long sea voyages and out-of-season use. The English word pickle first appears around 1400.

Baked dish made of a [[Pastry|pastry]] casing that contains a sweet or savory filling. Sweet pies may be filled with fruit, nuts, [[Fruit preserves|fruit preserves]] or custard, while savory pies may contain meat, eggs and cheese, or a mixture of meat and vegetables. A pie may have a pastry top and base, or only one. The English word first appears in 1303 in the expense accounts of Bolton Priory in [[Yorkshire]]. Early pies were crusty cakes of ground [[Wheat|wheat]] or [[Barley|barley]], containing honey. A recipe for chicken pie, written on a tablet in [[Sumer]], predates 2000 BC. The Romans covered meats with a plain pastry that was not meant to be eaten. By 160 BC, Marcus Porcius Cato described *placenta*, a pie resembling a cheesecake on a pastry base. With the Roman road network, pie cooking spread throughout [[Europe]].

German legend about a piper who leads the children of Hamelin away. The town, plagued by [[Rat|rats]], hires a piper in multicolored ("pied") clothing, who lures the rats into the Weser River. When the mayor refuses to pay the promised 1,000 guilders, the piper returns on St. John and Paul's day and leads away 130 children into a mountain cave. Other versions have them drowned in the river or taken to Transylvania. Some scholars see a record of eastward emigration during [[Middle Ages|medieval]] colonization of eastern Europe. The phrase "pied piper" describes someone who attracts followers through charisma or false promises.

Region of northwestern Italy (pop., 2026: 4,255,006), second in area only to [[Sicily]]. Covering 25,387.07 sq km, it borders France and Switzerland to the west and north, and the regions of Liguria, Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna and Aosta Valley. Its capital, [[Turin]], was the first capital of the [[Kingdom of Italy]], from 1861 to 1865. The name derives from Medieval Latin for "at the foot of the mountains," referring to the [[Alps]]. Piedmont was the heartland of the Savoy-led Kingdom of Sardinia and a springboard for Italian unification in 1859–61. Its hills produce renowned [[Wine|wines]], including Barolo.
